content: Granisetron, commonly marketed under the brand name Sancuso, is a medication used to prevent nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy. It is available as a transdermal patch that delivers the drug continuously over a period of time. Below is a detailed explanation of its usage, precautions, and potential side effects: Usage Instructions: Application Timing: Apply the patch 24 to 48 hours before starting chemotherapy. The patch should remain in place during chemotherapy and for at least 24 hours after the treatment ends. Do not wear the patch for more than 7 consecutive days. Application Site: Apply the patch to clean, dry, intact, and nearly hairless skin on the upper outer arm. Avoid areas that are red, irritated, damaged, or have been recently shaved. Do not apply the patch to areas where creams or lotions have been used. Handling: Do not cut the patch. Open the sealed pouch only when ready to use. After removing the patch, fold it in half with the sticky sides together and discard it safely to prevent accidental contact or ingestion by children or pets. Avoid exposing the patch and surrounding area to direct heat sources (e.g., heating pads, heat lamps) as this can increase drug absorption. Removal: Gently peel off the patch when it is time to remove it. Wash the application site and hands thoroughly with soap and water after removal. Precautions: Drug Interactions: Granisetron can prolong the QTc interval, increasing the risk of serious arrhythmias. Caution is advised when co-administering with other drugs that also prolong the QTc interval or increase serotonin levels, as this may lead to serotonin syndrome or toxicity. In some cases, alternative medications should be considered. Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: There is limited data on the use of granisetron during pregnancy and lactation. The potential risks to the fetus or breastfeeding infant are not well established. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the medication and any potential adverse effects on the infant. Liver Disease: Use with caution in patients with liver disease, as this may affect drug metabolism. Hypersensitivity: Avoid use in patients with known hypersensitivity to granisetron or its excipients. Side Effects: Common Side Effects: These include headache (10-21%), constipation (3-18%), diarrhea (1-9%), asthenia (5%), somnolence (10%), sedation (10%), and drowsiness (10%). Application site reactions such as pain, itching, redness, rash, irritation, or discoloration may also occur. Serious Side Effects: Granisetron may rarely cause serotonin syndrome, especially when used with other serotonergic drugs. Symptoms include agitation, hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, flushing, muscle rigidity, and gastrointestinal distress. Seek immediate medical attention if these occur. Cardiac Effects: QTc prolongation may lead to arrhythmias, particularly in patients with bradycardia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, or congenital QT prolongation. Monitor ECGs and electrolytes as clinically indicated. Allergic Reactions: Severe allergic reactions are rare but may include rash, itching/swelling, severe dizziness, or difficulty breathing. Special Considerations: Drug Interactions: Granisetron interacts with numerous medications, particularly those that also prolong the QTc interval or increase serotonin levels. In many cases, co-administration should be avoided, or alternative therapies should be used. Examples include ondansetron, fluoxetine, sertraline, and certain antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin, moxifloxacin). Monitoring: For patients requiring co-administration of QTc-prolonging drugs, frequent ECG monitoring is recommended. Discontinue use if the QTc interval exceeds 500 ms or if there is a significant change from baseline. Administration Notes: Storage: Keep the patch in its sealed pouch until ready to use. Store at room temperature away from heat and moisture. Patient Education: Patients should be instructed on proper application, removal, and disposal of the patch. They should also be advised to report any severe or persistent side effects to their healthcare provider. Granisetron is an effective antiemetic for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting when used as directed. However, its potential for QTc prolongation and serotonin-related toxicity necessitates careful monitoring and consideration of drug interactions.
